result: At physiological protein and lipid levels, HOPS- and SNARE-dependent fusion is stimulated by Sec17 and Sec18:ATP without requiring ATP hydrolysis. Fusion with ATPγS (non-hydrolyzable) is nearly as rapid as with ATP for the first 10 minutes, indicating that ATP hydrolysis is not required for the initial fusion stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C1, C48, C54-C56, C63, and C145 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figure 2A showing comparable fusion rates with ATP and ATPγS during the first 10 minutes. The use of physiological protein:lipid ratios (1:32,000 for SNAREs, 1:8000 for Ypt7) and physiological lipid compositions strengthens the conclusion. The distinction between fusion stimulation (ATP-independent) and cis-SNARE disassembly (ATP-dependent) is clearly demonstrated.

result: Sec17 requires both its N-terminal apolar loop and its central residues that bind the SNARE 0-layer for fusion stimulation with complete SNARE zippering. Mutations F21S,M22S (removing apolar character) and K159E,K163E (interfering with SNARE 0-layer interactions) both reduce fusion to baseline levels.
evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C76, and C77 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing that both Sec17-F21S,M22S and Sec17-K159E,K163E mutations reduce fusion to levels seen without Sec17. The functional importance of these domains is further validated by liposome binding assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) showing reduced SNARE association for the K159E,K163E mutant. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence supports this conclusion.

result: Adding a transmembrane anchor to Sec17 bypasses the requirement for the apolar loop when complete SNARE zippering occurs, suggesting the loop functions primarily for membrane binding rather than bilayer rearrangement under these conditions. TM-Sec17-F21S,M22S shows similar fusion activity as TM-Sec17 wild-type.
evaluation: Claims C4, C87, and C88 are supported by experimental data in Figures 4B-C showing that TM-Sec17-F21S,M22S stimulates fusion similarly to TM-Sec17 wild-type, contrasting with the loss of function seen with soluble Sec17-F21S,M22S (Figure 3A). This elegant bypass experiment provides strong evidence that the apolar loop's primary function with complete zippering is membrane anchoring. The inference in C5 and C109 is well-justified by the data.

result: When complete C-terminal SNARE zippering is prevented by Qc-3Δ truncation, fusion is blocked but can be restored by Sec17, Sec18, and ATPγS. This fusion strictly requires all three components (HOPS, Sec17, Sec18) and is lost upon omission of any one.
evaluation: Claims C6, C49, C50, C90-C92 are strongly supported by experimental data in Figures 5A-B. The Qc-3Δ mutation (deletion of 21 C-terminal residues) completely blocks fusion with ATP, but ATPγS restores substantial fusion. The strict requirement for each component is demonstrated by loss of fusion upon omission of HOPS, Sec17, or Sec18 (Figure 5B). This represents a distinct fusion mechanism from that with complete zippering.

result: When SNARE zippering is incomplete (Qc-3Δ), the Sec17 apolar loop has functions beyond membrane anchoring. TM-Sec17-F21S,M22S shows diminished fusion compared to TM-Sec17 wild-type with Qc-3Δ, indicating the apolar loop provides additional functionality beyond membrane binding.
evaluation: Claims C7, C51, C99-C101, and C108 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6C showing that with Qc-3Δ, TM-Sec17-F21S,M22S has reduced fusion activity compared to TM-Sec17 wild-type, even though both are membrane-anchored. This contrasts with the results for complete zippering (Figure 4C) where the FSMS mutation had no effect on TM-Sec17. The data support a dual function model for the apolar loop depending on zippering state.

result: Sec17 and Sec18 act twice in the fusion cycle: first binding to trans-SNARE complexes to accelerate fusion (ATP-independent), then hydrolyzing ATP to disassemble cis-SNARE complexes for SNARE recycling. ATP hydrolysis is strictly required for fusion of 4-SNARE proteoliposomes and enables multiple fusion rounds.
evaluation: Claims C8, C58, C78, C81, C82, and C146 are supported by converging evidence from Figures 2A-B and 3B. Figure 2A shows ATP-independent fusion stimulation (first 10 min with ATPγS), while Figure 2B demonstrates strict ATP requirement for 4-SNARE proteoliposome fusion (cis-SNARE disassembly). Figure 3B shows enhanced fusion at later times with ATP compared to ATPγS, supporting the recycling model. The dual function model is well-supported.

result: Fusion with incomplete SNARE zippering (Qc-3Δ) requires Sec17:Sec18 interactions and Sec17:SNARE interactions. The L291A,L292A mutation (affecting Sec17:Sec18 binding) markedly diminishes fusion, while F21S,M22S and K159E,K163E mutations abolish fusion. No fusion occurs with hydrolyzable ATP.
evaluation: Claims C95-C98, C120-C121 are supported by experimental data in Figures 6A-B showing differential effects of Sec17 mutations on fusion with Qc-3Δ and ATPγS. The L291A,L292A mutation reduces fusion, while F21S,M22S and K159E,K163E abolish it. The complete loss of fusion with ATP (Figure 6B) suggests ATP hydrolysis disrupts the partially-zippered intermediate. The inferences about required interactions are well-justified.

result: With arrested SNARE zippering (Qc-3Δ), omission of Sec17 during initial incubation allows formation of a productive intermediate that drives rapid fusion upon Sec17 addition. This intermediate requires HOPS, Sec18, ATPγS, and Qc-3Δ, suggesting an assembled but partially-zippered trans-SNARE complex with bound Sec18:ATPγS.
evaluation: Claims C102-C105 and C126 are supported by the staging experiment in Figure 7. Omission of Sec17 alone allows formation of an intermediate that fuses faster than the no-omission control upon Sec17 addition. Omission of Sec17 plus any other component prevents this enhanced fusion, indicating all other components are required for intermediate formation. The inference about the intermediate's composition (C105) is reasonable given the experimental design.

result: Sec17 and Sec18 stimulate fusion in an approximately additive manner with complete SNARE zippering, showing no synergy. The insensitivity to the Sec17-L291A,L292A mutation (which blocks Sec17:Sec18 interactions) reinforces this lack of synergy. Sec18 alone also stimulates fusion, with greater stimulation in the presence of ATP or ATPγS.
evaluation: Claims C74-C75, C61-C62, and C85 are supported by experimental data in Figures 2A and 3A. The combined addition of Sec17 and Sec18 gives approximately additive stimulation, and the Sec17-L291A,L292A mutation (which disrupts Sec17:Sec18 interaction) does not reduce fusion, indicating independent action. Sec18 alone stimulates fusion (Figure 2A), though the mechanism remains unclear. The observations are well-documented but the mechanistic understanding is incomplete.

result: The K159E,K163E and F21S,M22S mutations affect only the first fusion round (supported by ATPγS), not subsequent ATP-dependent SNARE recycling. Sec17 can support Sec18 and ATP-dependent SNARE recycling without the apolar loop or SNARE 0-layer interactions.
evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 showing similar diminution of fusion by these mutations with ATP or ATPγS, suggesting they only affect the first round. ATP-dependent recycling occurs with all Sec17 variants tested, indicating these domains are not required for the disassembly function. The inference is reasonable but relies on indirect evidence.

result: ATPγS has a positive role in fusion with Qc-3Δ beyond simply blocking ATP hydrolysis. Complete removal of ATP by glucose/hexokinase does not allow fusion with Qc-3Δ, indicating ATPγS actively promotes fusion.
evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5C showing that removal of all ATP by glucose/hexokinase prevents fusion with Qc-3Δ, while ATPγS supports fusion. This control experiment demonstrates that ATPγS functions as an activating ligand for Sec18 rather than simply preventing ATP hydrolysis. The experimental design is appropriate and the conclusion is well-supported.

result: The proteoliposome system uses physiological protein:lipid ratios (Ypt7 at 1:8000, SNAREs at 1:32,000) and achieves fusion rates resembling those of purified vacuoles, validating the reconstituted system as physiologically relevant.
evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by citations to Zick and Wickner, 2016 establishing these ratios as physiological, and comparisons to fusion rates with purified vacuoles (Haas et al., 1994; Nichols et al., 1997). The validation of the reconstituted system is important for interpreting the mechanistic findings. The protein:lipid ratios are dramatically lower than in previous studies, strengthening the physiological relevance.

result: Sec17-K159E,K163E has reduced capacity to synergistically associate with soluble SNAREs and bind to liposomes compared to wild-type Sec17 or Sec17-L291A,L292A, as shown by liposome floatation assays.
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing reduced liposome binding for Sec17-K159E,K163E compared to wild-type or L291A,L292A mutant. This biochemical assay validates the functional importance of the SNARE 0-layer interaction observed in fusion assays. The quantification in part B strengthens the conclusion.

result: ATP or ATPγS alone had no effect on HOPS-mediated fusion, while Sec17 alone gave small stimulation of HOPS-dependent fusion.
evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are supported by experimental data (not shown for ATP/ATPγS) and Figure 2A (filled triangles) for Sec17 stimulation. The citation to Zick et al., 2015 provides additional support. These observations establish baseline conditions for interpreting the combined effects of Sec17, Sec18, and nucleotides.

result: With ATP present, there is only partial diminution of fusion with Sec17-F21S,M22S or Sec17-K159E,K163E mutations, contrasting with the complete loss of stimulation seen with ATPγS.
evaluation: Claim C79 is supported by experimental data in Figure 3B showing partial reduction in fusion with these mutants when ATP is present. This contrasts with Figure 3A (ATPγS) where these mutations reduce fusion to baseline. The difference likely reflects ATP-dependent SNARE recycling compensating for reduced first-round fusion efficiency.

result: Two non-exclusive mechanistic models are proposed for Sec17 function: a 'Wedge Model' where the apolar loop inserts into bilayers to trigger fusion, and a 'trans-SNARE Stability Model' where Sec17 stabilizes fully-zippered trans-SNAREs. The models differ in emphasis but both involve membrane binding and SNARE interaction.
evaluation: Claims C106-C107, C110-C112, C116-C117, C122, C125, and C143 present speculative mechanistic models based on the experimental observations. While the data support dual functions for the apolar loop depending on zippering state, the molecular mechanisms remain unclear. The models are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct structural or biophysical evidence. Additional experiments (e.g., structural studies, FRET measurements) would be needed to distinguish between these models.

result: When C-terminal zippering is incomplete, TM-Sec17 supports fusion better than TM-Sec17-F21S,M22S, suggesting the apolar loop acts as a wedge. With full zippering, adding a membrane anchor bypasses the need for loop apolarity, suggesting the loop promotes membrane association.
evaluation: Claims C108-C109 are supported by comparing Figures 6C (incomplete zippering) and 4C (complete zippering). The differential effect of the FSMS mutation in TM-Sec17 depending on zippering state supports context-dependent functions for the apolar loop. However, the inference about 'wedge' function (C108) is speculative—the data show the loop is required but don't directly demonstrate bilayer perturbation.

result: The apolar loop and SNARE 0-layer interactions are important for disassembly of isolated neuronal SNARE complexes but may be less vital for vacuolar membrane-bound SNAREs in the presence of HOPS.
evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by citations to neuronal SNARE studies. Claim C84 is speculation based on the observation that these mutations don't prevent ATP-dependent recycling (Figure 3—figure supplement 4). However, the authors don't directly test disassembly efficiency with these mutants. The speculation is reasonable given HOPS's multiple affinities, but lacks direct experimental support in this study.

result: Studies by Winter et al. (2009) showed that membrane association of neuronal SNAREs enhances α-SNAP/NSF-mediated disassembly in an apolar loop-dependent manner, likely reflecting enhanced binding rather than wedge-like disruption.
evaluation: Claims C113-C115 accurately cite and interpret prior work (Winter et al., 2009; Ryu et al., 2015; Choi et al., 2016). The interpretation that the apolar loop enhances binding rather than causing bilayer disruption during disassembly is reasonable and consistent with the cited structural studies. This provides context for interpreting the current findings.

result: Background claims about membrane fusion machinery, including Rab GTPases, tethering complexes, SNAREs, SM proteins, and Sec17/Sec18, establish the biological context for the study.
evaluation: Claims C9-C28 represent established knowledge in the membrane fusion field, supported by appropriate citations to primary literature and reviews. These background claims are accurately stated and provide necessary context. Some claims (C27-C28) include speculative elements about SNARE function that are appropriately qualified.

result: Background information about the HOPS complex and vacuolar SNAREs, including HOPS structure, Rab binding, SM function, and Vam7 properties, establishes the specific system under study.
evaluation: Claims C29-C35 accurately describe the HOPS complex and vacuolar SNARE properties based on cited literature. These are well-established facts about the yeast vacuolar fusion machinery that provide essential background for interpreting the experimental results.

result: Prior studies of vacuole fusion using in vivo, purified organelle, and reconstituted systems have shown that Sec17 can restore fusion when SNARE zippering is incomplete and that high SNARE levels can mask fusion requirements.
evaluation: Claims C36-C47 accurately summarize prior work on vacuole fusion, including the authors' own studies and those of others (Schwartz and Merz, 2009; Xu et al., 2010; Lobingier et al., 2014; Zick et al., 2015). These claims establish the rationale for the current study's focus on physiological protein levels and provide context for interpreting the new findings.

result: Prior characterization of Sec17 mutants shows that F21S,M22S affects the apolar loop, L291A,L292A affects Sec18 interaction, and K159E,K163E affects SNARE 0-layer interaction. These mutants have distinct functional profiles in different assays.
evaluation: Claims C64-C70 accurately cite prior characterization of Sec17 mutants from multiple studies (Winter et al., 2009; Barnard et al., 1997; Schwartz and Merz, 2009; Zhao et al., 2015; Zick et al., 2015). The functional profiles described provide rationale for using these mutants to dissect Sec17 function in the current study.

result: The structural state of partially-zippered SNARE complexes is unclear, with prior studies suggesting either disorder (NMR in solution) or maintained structure (crystal packing). Other studies show Sec17/α-SNAP can stabilize zippered SNAREs or open C-terminal domains.
evaluation: Claims C118-C119, C123-C124 accurately acknowledge uncertainty about SNARE structure with incomplete zippering and cite relevant structural studies (Trimbuch et al., 2014; Kümmel et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2016; Ryu et al., 2015; Choi et al., 2016). This honest assessment of knowledge gaps and citation of potentially contradictory findings strengthens the discussion.

result: The working model describes the fusion cycle including cis-SNARE disassembly, tethering, fusion microdomain assembly through affinity networks, HOPS-catalyzed trans-SNARE assembly, SNARE zippering, and Sec17/Sec18 binding.
evaluation: Claims C127-C142 present a working model integrating the current findings with prior knowledge. Most elements are supported by cited literature. Some elements (C130, C142) involve speculation or inference. The model provides a useful framework for understanding the fusion cycle, though some details remain uncertain.

result: Summary of key findings and remaining questions: optimal fusion requires Sec17, Sec18, and complete zippering; ATP serves as activating ligand without requiring hydrolysis for fusion; ATP hydrolysis drives cis-SNARE disassembly; several mechanistic questions remain unresolved.
evaluation: Claims C144-C149 accurately summarize the main findings supported by the experimental data. Claims C147-C150 appropriately acknowledge remaining uncertainties and unanswered questions. The honest assessment of what is known versus unknown strengthens the scientific rigor of the discussion.

result: Comparison to earlier studies explains why previous work did not observe Sec17's role in fusion: high SNARE levels, non-physiological lipid compositions, and long lag times between docking and fusion may have obscured Sec17's contribution.
evaluation: Claims C151-C155 provide reasonable explanations for differences between current and prior findings, citing the authors' own earlier work (Zick et al., 2015; Mayer et al., 1996). The speculation in C155 is appropriately qualified. This reconciliation of apparently contradictory findings strengthens the overall narrative.
